title: Google Cloud Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Google Cloud Platform lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Meet Google Cloud
entries.summary: Google Cloud provides hosted services for computing, storage and data work. Begin by matching a service to a small, clear need.

example.code:
Need: store the files for a club page
Data: index.html, styles.css and logo.png
No need: visitor passwords or a custom database

notes: Cloud experiments may have costs; no resources are created by these lessons.

entries.name: Projects organise resources
entries.summary: A Google Cloud project groups resources and settings. It has a project name, a project ID and a project number with different roles.

example.code:
Display name: Club practice
Project ID: fictional-club-practice
Project number: assigned by the service

notes: A familiar display name is not enough to prove you selected the right project.

entries.name: Regions and zones
entries.summary: A region is a geographic area. A zone is a deployment area within a region. Some resources are zonal, regional or global.

example.code:
Region example: us-central1
Zone example: us-central1-a
Plan: check the location type of each service

notes: Do not assume every service uses a zone field.

entries.name: IAM roles and principals
entries.summary: A principal is an identity asking for access. An IAM role groups permissions, and a policy binds a role to principals at a resource scope.

example.code:
Principal: fictional reviewer
Role: an appropriate read-only role
Scope: the intended practice resource

notes: Do not grant owner access merely to bypass a permission error.

entries.name: Service accounts are workload identities
entries.summary: A service account represents an application or workload. It is different from a person's user account.

example.code:
Workload: approved report task
Identity: its own service account
Access: only the data needed for the report

notes: Avoid downloading long-lived keys when a supported keyless identity method fits the task.

entries.name: Cloud Storage objects
entries.summary: Cloud Storage keeps objects in buckets. An object name identifies the object within its bucket.

example.code:
Bucket: fictional-club-files
Object name: images/logo.png
Data: the logo file

notes: Decide access rules deliberately before making any object public.

entries.name: Object versions and lifecycle rules
entries.summary: Versioning and lifecycle rules can help retain or clean up object versions. They need a deliberate policy so useful data is not lost or kept forever.

example.code:
Keep current page files
Retain older versions for an agreed recovery period
Review lifecycle cleanup rules before enabling them

notes: A cleanup rule can delete data; inspect its scope before use.

entries.name: Compute Engine virtual machines
entries.summary: Compute Engine provides virtual machines. You choose a machine configuration, image and location and manage the guest software.

example.code:
Planned VM: one small learning instance
Image: a supported operating system
Owner work: patching, access and monitoring

notes: Stopping a VM does not necessarily remove charges for associated disks.

entries.name: VPC networks and subnets
entries.summary: Google Cloud VPC networks are global resources. Their subnets are regional. This is a useful distinction from some other cloud network models.

example.code:
VPC: club-network
Subnet: club-subnet in us-central1
Address range: 10.3.1.0/24

notes: Do not assume a VPC network itself belongs to just one region.

entries.name: Firewall rules control connections
entries.summary: VPC firewall rules allow or deny selected traffic for targeted resources. A good rule names the needed sources, protocol and ports.

example.code:
Target: intended practice web VM
Allowed: HTTPS on TCP 443 from approved sources
Administration: restricted separately

notes: A firewall rule cannot fix an insecure application by itself.

entries.name: Logging and Monitoring
entries.summary: Cloud Logging records supported events. Cloud Monitoring tracks metrics and alert conditions. Use both to understand a problem.

example.code:
Metric: failed requests per minute
Log event: one request could not find a file
Action: check the file path and deployment contents

notes: Do not log tokens or private messages to make diagnosis easier.

entries.name: Budgets and labels
entries.summary: Budgets help monitor spend and send notifications. Labels help group costs by project purpose. Neither is a reason to skip cost review.

example.code:
Label: purpose=learning
Fictional monthly budget: 6 units
Alert at half: 3 units

notes: Budget alerts do not automatically stop all Google Cloud spending.
